pronunciation.approximation: 'KAH-goo-tsoo-chee' — the 'tsu' is crisp, and the final 'chi' is like 'chee'.

kin.label: Japanese
kin.form: 迦具土 (Kagutsuchi), the fire god whose birth killed Izanami

pronunciation.note: Kagutsuchi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the volatile fire god whose birth marks the beginning of death in the world.

domains.title: God of Fire and Volcanic Force
domains.subtitle: Creation, Destruction, and the Origin of Death
domains.lead: Kagutsuchi is the fire god whose birth burned his mother Izanami to death, introducing mortality into the mythic world. He is creation and destruction in one figure: the flame that forges and the flame that consumes. After his death at the hands of Izanagi, his scattered body became the volcanoes and hot springs of Japan.

cards.name: Birth of Fire
cards.desc: His birth from Izanami introduced both fire and death into the world.

cards.name: Slain by Izanagi
cards.desc: Izanagi avenged Izanami's death by cutting Kagutsuchi into pieces.

cards.name: Volcano God
cards.desc: His body became the volcanoes and geothermal features of the land.

cards.name: Forge and Hearth
cards.desc: Fire for cooking, warmth, and metalwork descends from his power.

symbols.name: Sword
symbols.meaning: The weapon with which Izanagi slew him

symbols.name: Volcano
symbols.meaning: His dismembered body became Japan's volcanic peaks

symbols.name: Forge
symbols.meaning: The fire of the blacksmith and the hearth

mythology.lead: Kagutsuchi's mythology is brief but pivotal: his birth kills the creator goddess and sets in motion the separation of life and death.

myths.title: The Burning Birth
myths.text: When Izanami gave birth to Kagutsuchi, the fire god, his flames were so intense that they burned her genitals and killed her. From her dying body came further kami of mountains, rivers, and earth. Kagutsuchi thus became the first cause of death in the mythic world.

myths.title: Izanagi's Vengeance
myths.text: Grief-stricken and enraged, Izanagi drew his sword and cut Kagutsuchi into pieces. From the blood on his sword and from Kagutsuchi's body came numerous kami associated with swords, mountains, and water. The fire god's destruction paradoxically produced more life.

myths.title: Fire and the Hearth
myths.text: Despite his destructive origin, Kagutsuchi became a deity honored in hearth rituals and by blacksmiths. Fire could kill, but it also cooked food, warmed homes, and transformed metal. This double nature made him an object of both fear and reverence.

lore.syncretism: Kagutsuchi parallels fire gods in many traditions, but his role as the cause of the creator goddess's death is distinctive. In later Shinto and folk belief, he overlaps with hearth deities and volcanic kami. The Japanese archipelago's volcanic geology made fire gods perpetually relevant.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kagutsuchi appears in popular media as a volcanic or destructive deity, and his name is invoked in discussions of Japanese volcanism and geothermal energy. The ritual care of fire — in the hearth, the forge, and the volcano — preserves his ancient significance.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kagutsuchi is the fire we cannot live without and cannot fully control. His birth destroyed the world of innocence, but his death scattered the seeds of mountains and rivers. He reminds us that the energies that sustain us can also consume us.
lore.archaeology: Kagutsuchi has no major independent shrine. His importance is expressed in hearth rituals, blacksmith traditions, and the volcanic landscape of Japan itself, which preserves the memory of fire as both creative and destructive.
